    AI Overview
    The Mariana Islands are a crescent-shaped archipelago of 15 volcanic mountains in the northwestern Pacific Ocean, consisting of the U.S. territory of Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI). The capital is Saipan. These tropical islands are known for tourism, stunning beaches, and the nearby deep Mariana Trench. The population is concentrated on Saipan, Tinian, and Rota. 
    Geography and Climate 
    • Location: Situated south-southeast of Japan and west-northwest of Hawaii.
    • Island Types: The southern islands (including Saipan, Tinian, Rota) are made of limestone with coral reefs, while the northern islands are volcanic.
    • Climate: Tropical with a dry season from December to June and a rainy season from July to October.
    • Natural Hazards: The islands are subject to typhoons, particularly between June and December. 
    This video shows the impact of a super typhoon on the Mariana Islands:
    1m
    Nature Damage
    YouTube• Apr 14, 2026
    Major Islands and Population 
    • Total Population: The CNMI has a relatively small population, with over 90% residing on Saipan.
    • Major Islands: The primary population centers and tourist spots are Saipan, Tinian, and Rota.
    • Northern Islands: Include active volcanoes on Anatahan, Pagan, and Agrihan. 
    Culture and Tourism 
    • Government: The CNMI is an unincorporated territory of the United States in a political union.
    • Languages: English is the official language, though Chamorro and Carolinian are also spoken.
    • Currency: United States Dollar ($).
    • Tourism: Popular activities include diving, exploring WWII historic sites, and visiting beaches.
    • Economy: Heavily reliant on tourism and related services. 
    History 
    • Discovery: Spain claimed the islands in 1565.
    • WWII: The U.S. military took control in 1945.
    • Commonwealth: The CNMI entered into a covenant with the U.S. in the 1970s. 
    Key Sites 
    • Mariana Trench Marine National Monument: Protects submerged volcanoes and hydrothermal vents.
    • Saipan: Known for the beaches of Micro Beach and the historical Last Command Post.

    History. What is the history of the Mariana Islands?
    About this result
    Feedback
    An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
    AI Overview
    The Mariana Islands were first settled around 1500–1400 BCE by Austronesian migrants from Southeast Asia, developing a unique Chamorro culture. Colonized by Spain in 1668 after Magellan's 1521 arrival, the population declined due to disease and conflict. Following the 1898 Spanish-American War, the islands were split: Guam became a U.S. territory, while the Northern Marianas were sold to Germany, later occupied by Japan, and eventually became a U.S. Commonwealth in 1986. 
    Key Historical Periods
    • Ancient Period (c. 1500 BCE - 1521 CE):
      Early settlers used advanced voyaging canoes (flying proas) and built houses on latte stones. 
    • Spanish Colonization (1668–1898):
      Spain solidified control over the islands, bringing Catholicism and initiating the Spanish-Chamorro Wars. The archipelago was named Las Marianas in 1668. 
    • Division and Colonial Changes (1899–1944):
      Following the Spanish-American War, Guam was ceded to the USA, and the Northern Marianas were sold to Germany. Japan occupied the Northern Marianas during WWI (1914) and managed them as a League of Nations mandate until 1944. 
    • World War II (1944-1945):
      The U.S. liberated the islands from Japan in 1944, notably after the Battle of Saipan. 
    • U.S. Administration and Commonwealth Status:
      After WWII, the islands were part of the UN Trust Territory administered by the U.S. In 1975, the Northern Marianas opted for a political union with the U.S., becoming a Commonwealth (CNMI) in 1986, with residents holding U.S. citizenship. 
    Today, the archipelago remains politically divided into the territory of Guam and the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI).

      Major Islands. What are the major islands in the Mariana Islands?
      About this result

      An AI Overview is not available for this searchCan't generate an AI overview right now. Try again later.
      AI Overview
      The major islands in the Mariana Archipelago are Guam, Saipan, Tinian, and Rota. These four southern, primarily coralline islands house almost the entire population, with Guam as a US territory and Saipan, Tinian, and Rota as the primary islands within the US Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI). 
      Major Islands Usage Examples
      • Guam: The largest island, serving as a major US military hub (naval and air force) and a tourism center. 
      • Saipan: The capital and population center of the CNMI, known for resorts, tourism, and historical WWII sites. 
      • Tinian: Known for its role in WWII as the departure point for the atomic bomb flights; currently a quiet island with tourism and agriculture.
      • Rota: Known for its largely untouched nature, eco-tourism, beaches, and rugged, rural landscapes. 
      Other Notable Islands
      • Pagan: The largest of the largely uninhabited northern volcanic islands, though it has been evacuated due to volcanic activity. 
      • Farallon de Medinilla: A small, uninhabited island primarily used by the US military for bombing exercises. 
      Synonyms and Key Terminology
      • The Marianas: Often used to refer to the entire archipelago.
      • CNMI (Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands): Refers to the 14 islands north of Guam. 
      • Guåhan: The indigenous Chamorro name for Guam.
      • Luta: The indigenous Chamorro name for Rota.
      • Tin'an: The indigenous Chamorro name for Tinian.
      • Northern Islands/Volcanic Chain: Refers to the uninhabited northern volcanic group (e.g., Agrihan, Pagan, Asuncion). 
      The southern islands are generally flatter limestone islands, while the northern islands are younger and volcanic.

        AI Overview
        The capital of the Northern Mariana Islands (a U.S. commonwealth) is Saipan. While the entire island of Saipan serves as the administrative center and main population hub, specific government functions are located in Capital Hill, with the judicial center in Susupe. 
        Usage Examples & Context:
        • Location:
          Saipan is located in the Pacific Ocean, acting as the main commercial and governmental hub for the archipelago. 
        • Government:
          Saipan is recognized as the capital city where legislative and executive branches are housed. 
        • Tourism/Geography:
          As the largest island in the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI), it is a popular destination known for beaches, tropical climate, and history. 
        Synonyms/Related Terms: 
        • CNMI: Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands.
        • The Marianas: Often used interchangeably for the archipelago.
        • Saipan: Frequently synonymous with "the capital" in regional context.

          AI Overview
          The population of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands (CNMI) is approximately 42,900 to 44,000 as of 2025–2026, reflecting a decline from 47,329 in the 2020 Census. The vast majority (over 90%) of residents live on the main island of Saipan, with smaller populations on Tinian and Rota. 
          Key details regarding the population of the Northern Mariana Islands:
          • Population Trend:
            The population has significantly decreased from a peak over 69,000 in 2000, due to the end of the garment industry, economic challenges, and reduced tourism. 
          • Key Locations:
            Over 90% of the population resides on Saipan, with others on Tinian and Rota. 
          • Demographics:
            As of 2020, over 50% of the population was Asian, and about 33.6% was Pacific Islander. 
          • Median Age:
            The median age is approximately 38.8 years. 
          • Urbanization:
            The population is almost entirely urban, with roughly 92% living in urban areas. 
          Note: The Mariana Islands consist of the CNMI (a US Commonwealth) and Guam, but typically "population of the Mariana Islands" refers to the CNMI when excluding Guam.

            The Mariana Islands, also simply the Marianas, are a crescent-shaped archipelago comprising the summits of fifteen longitudinally oriented, mostly dormant volcanic mountains in the north-western Pacific Ocean, between the 12th and 21st parallels north and along the 145th meridian east.
            Source: Wikipedia

            Area: 1,036 km2 (400 mi2)
            Biome: Tropical and subtropical dry broadleaf forests
            Territories: Guam and the Northern Mariana Islands
